cards.meaning: Dealing with things in a sensible, practical way based on what actually works, rather than on theory or ideals.
cards.nuance: Usually a compliment that suggests good judgement. Used about yourself it can sound like an excuse for cutting corners.

uses.sentence: Let’s be pragmatic and ship the core feature now, then polish the settings page next sprint.
uses.tip: Use it to steer a group from the ideal plan to the doable one.

uses.where: Dinner with friends · planning a trip
uses.sentence: Pragmatically, we can’t do three cities in four days, so let’s pick two.
uses.tip: The adverb works well at the start of a sentence to signal a reality check.

uses.where: Email to a landlord · repair request
uses.sentence: A pragmatic solution would be to replace the seal now and review the whole boiler in spring.
uses.tip: Pairs naturally with solution, approach, choice and compromise.

origin.summary: From Greek pragmatikos, ‘fit for business’, built on pragma, ‘a deed or affair’. It reached English through Latin pragmaticus.

timeline.text: pragma, ‘thing done, business’, from prassein, ‘to do’.
Enters English, first in legal and official senses.
Mainly means practical and realistic.

cards.pitfall: Don’t mix it up with programmatic, which means following a program or done by code.

cards.meaning: Honest and direct, saying what you really think even when it isn’t comfortable.
cards.nuance: Warmer than blunt: it suggests honesty with good intent. A candid photo is one taken naturally, without posing.

uses.sentence: Can I be candid? The deck is strong, but the pricing slide will confuse people.
uses.tip: “Can I be candid?” is a polite way to warn someone that honest feedback is coming.

uses.where: Coffee with a friend · catching up
uses.sentence: She was really candid about how hard the first year with the baby had been.
uses.tip: Often used to praise someone for opening up.

uses.sentence: The memoir is candid and funny, and it never feels like it’s fishing for sympathy.
uses.tip: A good word for describing interviews, memoirs and conversations.

origin.summary: From Latin candidus, ‘white, shining, pure’. The idea of purity shifted to ‘free from bias’ and then to ‘frank’.

timeline.text: candidus, ‘white, bright’, from candere, ‘to shine’.
Used in English to mean white, then pure or fair-minded.
The modern sense of ‘frank, outspoken’ takes over.

cards.pitfall: Candid isn’t a license to be harsh: candid implies honesty with care, while blunt or brutal suggests not caring how it lands.

cards.meaning: Very careful and precise, paying close attention to every small detail.
cards.nuance: Almost always praise. If you mean someone is too careful, choose fussy or pedantic instead.

uses.sentence: Priya’s notes on the audit were meticulous, so we caught the error before it reached the client.
uses.tip: Strong praise for reviewers, editors, accountants and anyone who checks things.

uses.where: Visiting a friend · admiring their home
uses.sentence: He meticulously restored every chair in the apartment himself.
uses.tip: The adverb fits craft and hobbies: restored, planned, labeled.

uses.sentence: I keep meticulous records, which made handover painless when I changed teams.
uses.tip: Back it up with a concrete result so it doesn’t read as an empty claim.

origin.summary: From Latin meticulosus, ‘fearful, timid’, from metus, ‘fear’. Being afraid of mistakes slowly became being careful about details.

timeline.text: meticulosus, ‘full of fear’.
Appears in English meaning timid or fearful.
Takes on the modern sense of extremely careful, partly via French méticuleux.

cards.meaning: Seeming to be everywhere at the same time; extremely common.
cards.nuance: Often a little wry or tired, as if something is so common you can’t escape it. Fine in conversation if said lightly.

uses.sentence: QR menus are ubiquitous now, so customers already know how to use them.
uses.tip: Useful for saying something is so common it no longer needs explaining.

uses.sentence: Have you noticed how ubiquitous those electric scooters have become?
uses.tip: A playful way to complain about a trend.

uses.sentence: Smartphones are so ubiquitous that we forget how recently they arrived.
uses.tip: Strong as an opening line that sets up a contrast.

origin.summary: From Latin ubique, ‘everywhere’. The noun ubiquity came first, in religious debates about God being present everywhere.

timeline.text: ubique, ‘everywhere’, from ubi, ‘where’.
Ubiquity used in theology for being everywhere at once.
Ubiquitous becomes a general word for ‘found everywhere’.

cards.pitfall: Say it you-BIK-wit-us, starting with a ‘you’ sound, not ‘oo’.

cards.meaning: Lasting for only a very short time.
cards.nuance: Has a slightly poetic, wistful feel. In tech it simply means temporary, like disappearing messages.

uses.sentence: Stories are ephemeral, so put the key offer in the pinned post as well.
uses.tip: Handy for content or data that disappears after a while.

uses.sentence: Cherry blossom is so ephemeral, we have to come back next weekend before it’s gone.
uses.tip: Fits beautiful things that don’t last: blossom, sunsets, moods.

uses.where: Personal essay · reflecting on a trend
uses.sentence: Most viral fame is ephemeral; the people who last keep making things after the attention fades.
uses.tip: Contrasts nicely with words like lasting or enduring.

origin.summary: From Greek ephēmeros, ‘lasting only a day’, from epi, ‘on’, and hēmera, ‘day’. It was first used in English for short fevers.

timeline.text: ephēmeros, ‘for a day’.
Used in medicine for a fever lasting one day.
Widens to anything short-lived.

cards.pitfall: Don’t confuse it with ethereal, which means delicate and otherworldly, not short-lived.

cards.meaning: A small, subtle difference in meaning, feeling, tone or color.
cards.nuance: Saying something needs nuance politely suggests it is more complicated than it looks. Nuanced is praise for careful thinking.

uses.sentence: The headline number looks bad, but there’s nuance here: new users are actually happier.
uses.tip: “There’s nuance here” slows a group down before it jumps to conclusions.

uses.sentence: I liked that the film gave the villain a more nuanced story.
uses.tip: Nuanced is the most common everyday form.

uses.where: Message to a friend · heated debate
uses.sentence: Twitter isn’t the place for nuance, so let’s talk about it properly over coffee.
uses.tip: Use it to move a hard conversation somewhere better suited.

origin.summary: Borrowed from French nuance, ‘shade of color’, from nuer, ‘to shade’. That verb is usually traced to nue, ‘cloud’, from Latin nubes.

timeline.text: nubes, ‘cloud’, probably the distant source.
nuance, ‘a shade or gradation of color’.
Enters English for subtle shades of meaning.

cards.pitfall: Nuanced means carefully balanced, not vague; don’t use it to dodge giving a clear answer.

cards.meaning: Able to recover quickly from difficulty, shock or damage.
cards.nuance: Positive and hopeful. Be careful telling someone in pain to be resilient; it can sound like you’re dismissing their struggle.

uses.sentence: We need a more resilient setup, so one failed server doesn’t take the whole site down.
uses.tip: In tech it means systems that keep working when parts fail.

uses.where: Chatting with a parent · school drop-off
uses.sentence: Kids are more resilient than we think; she’d forgotten the fall by lunchtime.
uses.tip: A common, reassuring thing to say about children.

uses.sentence: That year taught me resilience more than any job I’ve had.
uses.tip: The noun resilience is everywhere in professional writing; pair it with a real story.

origin.summary: From Latin resilire, ‘to leap back, rebound’, from re-, ‘back’, and salire, ‘to jump’. It first described things springing back into shape.

timeline.text: resilire, ‘to jump back’.
Used in English for physical rebounding.
Applied to people bouncing back from hardship.

cards.pitfall: Resilient means bouncing back after a hit; resistant means not being affected in the first place.

cards.meaning: Having mixed or opposite feelings about something at the same time.
cards.nuance: An honest, grown-up way to say you’re torn. It signals conflict, not lack of interest.

uses.sentence: I’m ambivalent about open desks: they help us talk, but focus time suffers.
uses.tip: Follow it with both sides of your feeling.

uses.sentence: Honestly, I’m ambivalent about the move; I’m excited but I’ll miss everyone.
uses.tip: Good for life decisions where you feel two things at once.

uses.sentence: The ending left me ambivalent, impressed by its nerve but unsure it earned it.
uses.tip: Reviewers use it to give a fair, two-sided reaction.

origin.summary: Coined in German as Ambivalenz by the Swiss psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler around 1910, from Latin ambi-, ‘both’, and valentia, ‘strength’.

timeline.text: ambi-, ‘both’, and valere, ‘to be strong’.
Bleuler uses Ambivalenz for conflicting feelings in psychiatry.
Everyday word for mixed feelings.

cards.pitfall: It doesn’t mean indifferent (not caring) or ambiguous (unclear in meaning); ambivalent means caring in two directions.

cards.meaning: Refusing to give up; holding on firmly to a goal, idea or grip.
cards.nuance: Admiring, with a hint of stubbornness. Stronger and more active than patient.

uses.where: Sales team call · celebrating a deal
uses.sentence: Sam was tenacious with that client, and after six months of follow-ups they finally signed.
uses.tip: Great for praising persistence without calling someone pushy.

uses.sentence: Their goalkeeper is tenacious; he never gives up on a ball.
uses.tip: Common in sports talk about defenders and underdogs.

uses.sentence: She tackled problems with real tenacity and never left a bug half-fixed.
uses.tip: The noun tenacity reads well in recommendations.

origin.summary: From Latin tenax, ‘holding fast’, from tenere, ‘to hold’, the same root as tenant and retain.

timeline.text: tenere, ‘to hold’; tenax, ‘gripping’.
Enters English for things that grip or stick.
Mostly describes determined people.

cards.pitfall: Don’t confuse it with tenuous, which means weak or flimsy, as in a tenuous link.

cards.meaning: Careful with money or resources, avoiding waste and unnecessary spending.
cards.nuance: A respectful word for saving. Cheap and stingy are the insulting versions.

uses.sentence: We’ll need to be frugal with travel this quarter and hold most meetings online.
uses.tip: A neutral way to announce cost-cutting.

uses.where: Chatting with a roommate · saving up
uses.sentence: I’m being frugal until the trip, so it’s home-cooked dinners for me.
uses.tip: Sounds disciplined rather than broke.

uses.sentence: This frugal soup uses up whatever vegetables are left at the end of the week.
uses.tip: Also describes meals or lifestyles that are simple and inexpensive.

origin.summary: From Latin frugalis, ‘economical’, from frux, ‘fruit, produce’, and so ‘value, worth’.

timeline.text: frux, ‘fruit, produce’; frugalis, ‘thrifty’.
Enters English meaning economical.
Common for careful spending and simple living.

cards.pitfall: Frugal is respectful; cheap and stingy are insults. Don’t say frugal when you mean someone never pays their share.

cards.meaning: Enjoying the company of other people; sociable and outgoing.
cards.nuance: Warm and positive. A bit more formal than outgoing, so it can sound playful in casual talk.

uses.sentence: He’s gregarious and great with clients, but we should check he enjoys deep solo work too.
uses.tip: Useful when describing personality fit.

uses.sentence: You’ll love Maya, she’s the most gregarious person I know.
uses.tip: A flattering way to describe a friend who knows everyone.

uses.sentence: Starlings are gregarious birds, gathering in huge flocks over winter.
uses.tip: In biology it means living in groups, the word’s original sense.

origin.summary: From Latin gregarius, ‘belonging to a flock’, from grex, ‘flock, herd’, the same root as congregate and aggregate.

timeline.text: grex, greg-, ‘flock, herd’.
Enters English for animals that live in flocks.
Used for sociable people.

cards.meaning: The luck of finding something good or useful when you weren’t looking for it.
cards.nuance: Feels charming and a little magical. Works best for happy accidents, not just any good luck.

uses.sentence: It was pure serendipity: I sat next to their CTO at a wedding and we ended up partnering.
uses.tip: “Pure serendipity” is the classic phrase.

uses.sentence: We met by a serendipitous mix-up over who had booked the last table.
uses.tip: The adjective serendipitous suits meet-cute stories.

uses.where: Travel blog · a day in Lisbon
uses.sentence: Leave room in your plans for serendipity; my best meal came from a wrong turn.
uses.tip: Good advice-style line in travel writing.

origin.summary: Coined by the writer Horace Walpole in a 1754 letter, inspired by the tale The Three Princes of Serendip, whose heroes kept making lucky discoveries. Serendip is an old name for Sri Lanka.

timeline.text: The Three Princes of Serendip, known in Europe through translations.
Walpole coins serendipity in a letter.
Becomes widely used, especially for scientific discoveries.

cards.pitfall: It isn’t just luck; it is finding something good while looking for something else, or nothing at all.
